title: When Success Becomes Your Greatest Danger
paragraphs:
When Success Becomes Your Greatest Danger
The Lesson I Learned From King Asa's Final Years—and Why Finishing Well Matters More Than Starting Strong
There are stories in Scripture that inspire us.
Then there are stories that quietly dismantle our confidence.
King Asa's story does both.

Most believers remember Asa as one of Judah's greatest kings. He tore down idols. He called the nation back to the worship of the LORD. He led revival. He trusted God against impossible odds. His reign began with extraordinary faith, courageous obedience, and unmistakable blessing.
Yet Scripture refuses to end his biography where we would have preferred.
Instead, God allows us to watch a faithful king slowly drift—not into open idolatry, but into something more subtle, more relatable, and perhaps more dangerous.
Self-reliance.
It is one of the most heartbreaking endings in the Old Testament because it reminds every believer of an uncomfortable truth:
Starting well is a gift.
Finishing well is a lifelong surrender.
If that realization unsettles you, keep reading.
Because King Asa's final years may reveal something about our own hearts that we desperately need to see before it's too late.
A King Who Began With Extraordinary Faith
The chronicler introduces Asa as a king who "did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God" (2 Chronicles 14:2).
The Hebrew says:

טוֹב וְהַיָּשָׁר
(ṭôḇ wehayyāšār)
Literally,
"good and upright."
This was not merely political competence.
This described covenant faithfulness.
Asa removed pagan altars.
He destroyed sacred pillars.
He cut down the Asherah poles.
He commanded Judah to seek the LORD.
The Hebrew verb used repeatedly is דָּרַשׁ (dārash).
It means far more than simply "look for."
It means:

to diligently seek,
to inquire after,
to pursue with intentional devotion.
Seeking God was not a Sunday activity.
It became the culture of the kingdom.
And God responded.
When the Ethiopian army invaded with what Scripture describes as over a million soldiers (2 Chronicles 14:9), Judah had every earthly reason to surrender.
Instead, Asa prayed.
His prayer remains one of the most beautiful declarations of dependence in the Old Testament.
"LORD, there is none besides You to help between the mighty and the weak. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on You..." (2 Chronicles 14:11).
The phrase "we rely" comes from the Hebrew:

נִשְׁעַן
(nišʿan)
It means:
to lean one's full weight upon.
Not partial trust.
Complete dependence.
Asa won because he understood something every disciple of Christ must learn:
Victory never begins with our strength.
It begins with our surrender.
The Prophecy That Every Successful Christian Needs to Hear
After the victory, the prophet Azariah delivered one of the most overlooked messages in Scripture.
"The LORD is with you while you are with Him. If you seek Him, He will let you find Him..." (2 Chronicles 15:2).
Again, the Hebrew verb דָּרַשׁ (dārash) appears.
God was not teaching salvation by works.
He was describing covenant relationship.
A heart that continually pursues God experiences continual fellowship with God.
The warning was equally clear.
"If you forsake Him, He will forsake you."
Not because God becomes unfaithful.
But because persistent rebellion rejects His fellowship.
Asa listened.
He removed more idols.
He renewed the covenant.
The people rejoiced.
Everything appeared to be moving upward.
Which is often where the greatest spiritual danger begins.
Success Can Quietly Replace Dependence
Thirty-five years later, another crisis arrived.
This time, King Baasha of Israel fortified Ramah, threatening Judah's security (2 Chronicles 16).
Years earlier, Asa had run to God.
Now he ran somewhere else.
He emptied the treasures from the Temple.
He purchased military assistance from Syria.
Politically?
It worked.
Spiritually?
It exposed something heartbreaking.
The prophet Hanani confronted Asa.
His words still echo across generations.
"Because you relied on the king of Syria and did not rely on the LORD your God..." (2 Chronicles 16:7).
Again, the Hebrew root is שָׁעַן (sha'an).
Lean.
Depend.
Rest your weight upon.
Asa had simply shifted what carried his confidence.
Earlier, he leaned on God.
Now he leaned on strategy.
On diplomacy.
On human solutions.
The tragedy was not that military alliances existed.
The tragedy was that Asa never sought the LORD first.
How often do we do the same?
We pray less because experience has taught us enough.
We seek advice before Scripture.
We trust savings before providence.
We believe our planning is replacing our praying.
The danger is rarely abandoning God overnight.
The danger is slowly learning to function without needing Him.
The Verse That Pierces Every Heart
Then comes one of the greatest statements in all of Scripture.
"For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose heart is completely His."
(2 Chronicles 16:9)
The Hebrew phrase:

לֵבָב שָׁלֵם
(lēḇāḇ shālēm)
Literally means:
"a whole heart."
Not a perfect heart.
A fully devoted one.
The word שָׁלֵם (shalem) shares the same root family as שָׁלוֹם (shalom).
It carries ideas of completeness, wholeness, integrity, and undivided loyalty.
God is not searching for flawless people.
He is searching for fully surrendered hearts.
That changes everything.
When Correction Becomes an Enemy
Instead of repenting...
Asa imprisoned the prophet.
The Hebrew verb:

וַיִּכְעַס
(wayyik'as)
describes intense anger, provocation, and deep resentment.
Success had made him unable to receive correction.
This may be one of the most dangerous conditions a Christian can reach.
When conviction feels offensive instead of loving.
When accountability feels threatening instead of protective.
When anyone questioning us immediately becomes our enemy.
Hebrews later reminds believers,
"The Lord disciplines the one He loves" (Hebrews 12:6).
The Greek verb is:

παιδεύω
(paideuō)
It means:

to train,
to educate,
to lovingly discipline as a father shapes a child.
God's correction has never been evidence of rejection.
It is evidence of adoption.
Even His Illness Became a Spiritual Mirror
Near the end of his life, Asa developed a severe disease in his feet.
The Chronicler records something striking.
"Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians."
(2 Chronicles 16:12)
This verse has often been misunderstood.
Scripture is not condemning physicians.
Elsewhere, faithful medical care is treated positively (see Luke, "the beloved physician," in Colossians 4:14).
The issue is the contrast.
"He did not seek the LORD."
The Hebrew again uses דָּרַשׁ (dārash).
His greatest disease was not in his feet.
It was the absence of dependence.
Seeking medical help is not a lack of faith.
Ignoring God while doing so is.
Faith and wise treatment are never enemies.
They are meant to walk together.
Asa's Story Finds Its Answer in Jesus
King Asa leaves us with a question no human king could answer:
How can anyone finish faithfully?
The New Testament points us to Christ.
Jesus is everything Asa ultimately failed to be.
Where Asa gradually trusted himself...
Jesus continually trusted His Father.
Where Asa resisted correction...
Jesus humbled Himself, "becoming obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:8).
Where Asa leaned on political alliances...
Jesus prayed in Gethsemane,
"Not My will, but Yours, be done."
The Greek word translated "will" is:

θέλημα
(thelēma)
It refers to God's purposeful desire and sovereign intention.
Jesus submitted perfectly to the Father's will where every human ruler had fallen short.
And because Christ remained perfectly faithful, those who trust Him are not left to finish the race by their own strength.
The apostle Paul writes,
"He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion..." (Philippians 1:6).
The Christian life has never been sustained by human determination.
It has always been sustained by divine grace.
The Lesson I Cannot Forget
King Asa did not wake up one morning planning to drift.
Rarely does anyone.
Drift happens quietly.
Prayer becomes shorter.
Repentance becomes rarer.
Conviction becomes easier to ignore.
Success becomes easier to trust.
Dependence slowly disappears.
Perhaps that is why Asa's story feels so painfully modern.
Many believers today still attend church.
Still serve.
Still know Scripture.
Yet inwardly they have begun leaning on experience instead of Christ.
The warning is not written to shame us.
It is written to rescue us.
Today, the invitation remains exactly the same.
Lean again.
Seek again.
Depend again.
Because the God whose eyes searched the earth in Asa's day is still searching today—not for impressive résumés, polished ministries, or flawless reputations, but for hearts that are wholly His.
Sit with the Lord. Let Him search you as David prayed: "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalm 139:23). Your testimony may encourage another believer who is fighting the same unseen battle.
Sometimes God uses one faithful reminder to awaken a heart that has been slowly drifting.

If this article strengthened your walk with Christ, consider saving it so you can return to these Scriptures in seasons when success tempts you toward self-reliance. We never know whose life may be changed by a single act of faithful witness.
One surrendered heart can become the beginning of a rewritten life.
